new_entities.name: Tea consumption
aliases: black, green, oolong, or mate tea intake
new_entities.description: Habitual consumption of non-herbal tea beverages.

edges.effect_quant: The thyroid-cancer literature on tea is split: one older meta-analysis suggested modest protection, while large prospective cohorts were mostly null except for subgroup findings by menopausal status or histology.
edges.population: general adults with habitual tea consumption
edges.mechanism: Tea polyphenols may influence oxidative stress and thyroid-cell signaling, but any true effect seems to depend on subtype, dose, and hormonal context rather than showing up as a clean universal signal.
edges.summary: This edge is more unsettled than the mechanistic story would make you hope. The 2015 meta-analysis leaned protective, but the EPIC cohort was essentially null overall and the Japanese cohort split in opposite directions by menopausal status, so the most defensible label is mixed evidence.
edges.caveats: Tea subtype is a major issue here, and some of the more intriguing findings appear only in subgroup analyses. That keeps this from being a trustworthy prevention claim despite a plausible biologic rationale.
